screens.title: The Arduino Uno Board and Its Pinout
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll tour the Arduino Uno hardware so you can wire and program circuits with confidence. The Uno uses the ATmega328P microcontroller as its brain; it runs at sixteen megahertz and stores programs in flash memory while using SRAM for active variables and EEPROM for small persistent values. You'll learn how to recognize digital pins, analog inputs, PWM-capable pins, and the power rails so you can choose the right connection for LEDs, sensors, and small modules. We'll also highlight important safety rules: the board operates at five volts, pins have safe current limits, and certain pins are shared with serial communication. As you learn each part, you'll practice labeling a pinout diagram and answering quick checks that confirm you know which pins to use for which tasks. By the end of this chapter you will be able to read a pinout, identify PWM and analog pins, and explain why mixing three-volt and five-volt connections or overloading a pin can harm the board. Think about a small LED blink project you might build — understanding the pinout makes that first wiring step reliable and repeatable.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide what you'll be able to do after this chapter. First, you'll identify the main components on the Uno so you can point to the microcontroller, USB connector, power jack, and common headers. That skill matters because recognizing parts prevents miswiring. Second, you'll distinguish pin types: digital, analog inputs, power rails, and ground. Practically, this prevents connecting a sensor to the wrong pin and saves time troubleshooting. Third, you'll understand pin capabilities such as PWM for variable outputs, serial communication that shares pins zero and one, and the idea of interrupts so you can choose pins suitable for responsive events. Lastly, you'll be able to read a simple pinout diagram and label PWM pins, analog pins, the five-volt rail, and ground. Each objective includes a short verification milestone so you know when you're ready to move on. A common misconception is thinking all pins are identical; in reality, pins have different electrical roles. Keep that in mind as you practice labeling and wiring a basic LED circuit during the hands-on activity.

screens.title: How you'll practice these objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide shows how you'll practice and verify the skills. You'll print or open an Uno pinout diagram, then label PWM pins, analog inputs, the five-volt rail, and at least two ground pins as a hands-on activity. That practice converts recognition into habit so wiring becomes quicker and safer. You'll also run a simple LED blink test on pin thirteen because the onboard LED provides an immediate confirmation the board and code are working. For PWM practice you'll dim an LED on a PWM-supported pin and observe the analog-like brightness change; this demonstrates how PWM produces a variable output from a digital pin. Finally, you'll answer short assessment questions: which pins support PWM, what's the maximum safe current per pin, and what voltage a HIGH signal represents on an Uno. Checking these answers protects your board and reinforces correct wiring choices. A common misconception is assuming the five-volt pin can safely power motors; in practice you should avoid using the board's five-volt rail for high-current devices.

screens.title: ATmega328P: the Uno's microcontroller
screens.narratorSegment: The ATmega328P is the central microcontroller on the Uno that executes your programs and controls pins. Conceptually, it contains program memory where your sketch is stored, working memory used for variables when the program runs, and a small persistent storage area for values that must survive power cycles. The chapter lists the memory layout: thirty-two kilobytes of flash for program storage, two kilobytes of SRAM for runtime variables, and one kilobyte of EEPROM for persistent data. The chip runs at sixteen megahertz and operates at five volts, meaning its digital HIGH is five volts and LOW is zero volts. A concrete example: when you upload an LED blink sketch, the compiled program lives in flash. As the program runs, counters and state variables live in SRAM. If you want to save a configuration value that remains after a restart, you write it into EEPROM. A common beginner misconception is assuming the microcontroller can safely source large currents for motors or other actuators; the chip's input and output pins are limited in current and must be respected to avoid permanent damage. Takeaway: the ATmega328P is the board's decision maker and its memory and voltage domain shape both how you write programs and how you wire hardware.

keyIdea.title: Microcontroller overview
keyIdea.text: ATmega328P hosts your program, uses SRAM for runtime, and EEPROM for saved values; it runs at 5V and 16 MHz.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › ATmega328P
ATmega328P: definition and role
The microcontroller stores and runs your program and controls I/O at a five-volt domain.
Memory summary
32 KB flash for programs, 2 KB SRAM for variables, 1 KB EEPROM for persistent data.
Clock & Voltage
Runs at 16 MHz and operates at 5V, so digital HIGH equals five volts.
Practical example
A blink sketch is stored in flash; counters run in SRAM, and settings can be saved to EEPROM when needed.
Key Takeaway

The ATmega328P defines the Uno's capabilities: memory, clock speed, and operating voltage determine both code behavior and wiring constraints.

Annotated notes
  • Flash stores your sketch until you overwrite it.
  • SRAM holds variables while the sketch runs; limited space means be mindful of large arrays.
  • EEPROM persists small data between power cycles.
Common misconception
Believing the microcontroller can safely power high-current devices. In reality, per-pin current is limited and motors need external drivers and power.
Check your understanding
If a configuration must survive a restart where would you store it? How does the operating voltage affect sensor selection?

screens.title: Digital pins and their roles
screens.narratorSegment: The Uno exposes fourteen digital input/output pins numbered zero through thirteen. These pins can be used to read switches, drive LEDs, or control modules by setting them HIGH or LOW. A crucial detail: pins zero and one are also connected to the board's serial communication with the computer. That means when you use the serial port for debugging or upload sketches, those pins may be busy; beginners should avoid using them for other tasks when possible to prevent conflicts. Some pins offer additional capabilities — for example, a subset supports Pulse Width Modulation which we'll cover separately — but the base ability of digital pins is to act as a binary input or output at five volts. A concrete example: to turn an LED on you set its pin HIGH and provide a resistor to limit current; to read a pushbutton you configure a pin as input and check whether it reads HIGH when pressed. A common mistake is assuming any digital pin is suitable for serial communication; only pins zero and one are linked to the onboard serial lines. Closing question: which pins would you avoid using if you plan to use serial debugging during development?

keyIdea.text: Pins 0–13 are digital I/O; avoid using pins 0 and 1 when relying on serial communication to prevent conflicts.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Digital pins
Digital pins 0–13
Binary I/O usable for switches, LEDs, and modules at five volts.
Pin count
Fourteen pins labeled 0 through 13 provide digital input or output functionality.
Serial pins caution
Pins 0 and 1 are used for serial communication; avoid reusing them if you plan to monitor serial output or upload frequently.
Practical example
Use any available digital pin to blink an LED, but prefer other pins if you need serial debugging on the USB connection.
Common mistakes
  • Connecting a sensor that requires analog sensing to a digital-only pin expecting 0 or 5V.
  • Using pins 0 or 1 for an output while expecting serial data to arrive reliably.
Check
Before wiring, decide whether you'll use serial. If yes, leave 0 and 1 unused.

screens.title: Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) on the Uno
screens.narratorSegment: Pulse Width Modulation, or PWM, lets a digital pin mimic analog voltage by switching rapidly between HIGH and LOW. On the Uno, pins three, five, six, nine, ten, and eleven are PWM-capable, typically marked with a tilde. The microcontroller alternates the pin between five volts and zero volts at a fixed frequency, but varies the proportion of time the signal is HIGH versus LOW — that proportion is called duty cycle. When an LED is driven by a PWM pin, a higher duty cycle produces a brighter apparent output because the LED is on for a larger fraction of each cycle. A concrete example: to dim an LED smoothly, you write different duty cycles to a PWM pin and observe brightness change, which looks like analog variation though the pin is digital. A common misconception is that PWM outputs are true analog voltages; in fact they are digital pulses averaged by the LED or a filter to appear analog. A safety note: the pin still obeys current limits, so use an appropriate resistor and avoid drawing excessive current. Takeaway: PWM expands what digital pins can do, letting you control LED brightness or motor speed with careful duty-cycle changes.

keyIdea.title: PWM in practice
keyIdea.text: PWM uses rapid on/off switching and duty cycle control; use PWM pins (~3,5,6,9,10,11) for dimming and analog-like outputs.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Pulse Width Modulation
How PWM works
Digital pulses vary duty cycle to produce analog-like results.
PWM pins: ~3,5,6,9,10,11
Duty cycle: percent of time signal is HIGH
Use case: LED dimming or controlling perceived motor speed with drivers
Example
Write increasing duty cycles to a PWM pin to make an LED appear to ramp brighter. Include a resistor and respect per-pin current limits.
Misconception
PWM is not a steady analog voltage; components or filters average the pulses into an effective level.
Step-by-step: dim an LED
  1. Choose a PWM-capable pin marked with a tilde.
  2. Place the LED with a series resistor to the pin and ground.
  3. Set up the sketch to write varying duty cycles and upload.
  4. Observe brightness change and avoid exceeding 20 milliamps for safety.
Key Takeaway

PWM lets digital pins emulate analog outputs by changing duty cycle; always respect current limits and use correct pins.

screens.title: Analog input pins (A0–A5) and the ADC
screens.narratorSegment: The Uno provides six analog input pins labeled A0 through A5. These pins measure a voltage between zero and five volts and convert that voltage into a numeric value using a ten-bit Analog-to-Digital Converter. The conversion maps the measured voltage to a number between zero and one thousand twenty-three. For example, a sensor that outputs two and a half volts would read around halfway through the scale, producing a value close to five hundred. While called analog inputs, these pins can also be used as general-purpose digital pins if you need extra digital input and output. A practical use case is reading a variable resistor or a light sensor to produce values you can use in code to make decisions. A misconception is assuming analog inputs provide infinite precision; because the ADC is ten-bit, it provides discrete steps and not a perfectly smooth voltage reading. Key practice: always ensure the sensor voltage stays in the zero-to-five-volt range; exceeding that range risks damaging the microcontroller. Closing question: how would you convert the ADC reading back into a voltage in your application?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Analog inputs
Analog inputs A0–A5 and ADC
Measure voltages with a 10-bit converter producing values 0–1023.
ADC details
Ten-bit resolution maps 0–5V to 0–1023 discrete steps.
Example
A sensor reading of about 512 corresponds to roughly 2.5 volts; use that value in code to set thresholds or scaling.
Practical notes
  • Analog pins accept 0–5V. Never expose them to higher voltages.
  • They can double as digital I/O when analog input is not required.
  • Remember discrete steps: sensor noise or small changes may not move the ADC value if they are below one step.
Key Takeaway

Use A0–A5 to read sensors as 0–1023 values; convert back to volts when you need real-world units and protect pins from over-voltage.

screens.title: Power pins, connectors, and onboard hardware
screens.narratorSegment: The Uno's power section supplies the voltages your components need and offers multiple connectors. There are 5-volt and 3.3-volt pins used to power small sensors and modules, and several ground pins to complete circuits. The board can be powered over the USB-B connector or an external barrel jack. A power LED indicates when the board has power, and a reset button forces the microcontroller to restart a loaded program. Additional hardware includes ICSP headers used for advanced programming and the small LED connected to digital pin thirteen for quick testing. Practically, use the five-volt pin for low-current modules and prefer separate power supplies for motors or high-current devices. The USB connector is convenient for programming and low-current power, while the barrel jack supports higher external voltages via the board's regulator. A common beginner mistake is confusing the 3.3-volt pin with the 5-volt rail; some modules require three-point-three volts and can be damaged by five. Takeaway: know which connector you use for power and keep device current needs in mind when choosing a rail or external supply. Power pins, connectors, and onboard hardware means use 5v and 3.3v carefully and prefer external power for motors; the usb and barrel jack are common power sources with different capabilities.. In practical terms, 5v, 3.3v, gnd rails, usb-b, barrel jack, reset, and indicators. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Power & Connectors
Power rails and connectors
5V and 3.3V rails, multiple GND pins, USB-B, and barrel jack provide power options.
5V pin: useful for small components but not high-current devices like motors.
3.3V pin: for modules that require lower voltage; do not substitute 5V for 3.3V modules.
USB-B connector: convenient for programming and low-current powering.
Barrel jack: external power via regulator for higher current or voltage sources.
Onboard features
  • Reset button to restart the program immediately.
  • ICSP headers for advanced programming of the microcontroller.
  • Power LED to show board is powered and onboard LED wired to pin 13 for testing.
Key Takeaway

Choose the right power source and rail for the current your devices require and never assume a rail can drive motors without a separate driver and power supply.

screens.title: Current limits and safe wiring
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding current limits is essential to avoid damaging the Uno. The microcontroller's input/output pins can source or sink up to forty milliamps as an absolute maximum, but the recommended safe limit is around twenty milliamps per pin. Drawing more than the recommended amount can overheat and permanently damage the microcontroller. Practically, this means small indicator LEDs and low-current sensors are safe to run directly from a pin with a proper series resistor. However, motors, solenoids, or high-current LEDs require external drivers and a dedicated power supply. The chapter warns against powering high-current devices from the five-volt pin on the board; that rail is intended for low-current accessories. A typical beginner mistake is relying on a single pin to both power and control a high-current device — instead, use the pin only to switch a driver or transistor that supplies current from a separate supply. Takeaway: always check current draw of components, include resistors for LEDs, and prefer external power for anything with significant current demands. Current limits and safe wiring means pins tolerate 40 ma max but 20 ma is recommended. use drivers and external supplies for motors or high-current devices.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Current limits
Per-pin currents and recommendations
Use 20 milliamps as a safe working limit; forty milliamps is the absolute max.
LEDs: include a resistor and aim for ≤20 mA from a pin.
Motors: use driver circuits and an external power supply rather than the 5V pin.
Modules: check their current draw; many small sensors are fine on 5V but verify specification before connecting.
Practical wiring checklist
  1. Estimate the current each component draws.
  2. If any device draws more than 20 mA, use a driver or separate power supply.
  3. Never draw motor starting currents directly from an I/O pin or the onboard 5V rail.
Common mistake

Attempting to power motors from the Uno's 5V pin can overload the board and cause voltage drops or damage. Always separate control and power when current is high.

screens.title: Serial communication and shared pins
screens.narratorSegment: Serial communication allows the Uno to send and receive data with a computer or other devices. On the Uno, the hardware serial lines connect to digital pins zero and one. Because the USB interface uses those same lines for uploading sketches and for the serial monitor, using pins zero and one for other tasks can cause conflicts or confusing behavior when you try to program or debug your sketch. A concrete example: if you wire a sensor output to pin one and also open the serial monitor, the data stream can interfere and produce garbled output or prevent uploads. A common beginner misconception is assuming serial communication can be assigned to any free digital pin without consequence. While software serial libraries let you emulate serial on other pins, the hardware serial lines remain on pins zero and one and are best left free during development. Also, the learning objectives mention interrupts; while the chapter does not list specific interrupt-capable pins, interrupts let the microcontroller respond to external events immediately rather than polling. Follow a systematic routine to avoid common wiring mistakes.

In this lesson we'll tour the Arduino Uno hardware so you can wire and program circuits with confidence. The Uno uses the ATmega328P microcontroller as its brain; it runs at sixteen megahertz and stores programs in flash memory while using SRAM for active variables and EEPROM for small persistent values. You'll learn how to recognize digital pins, analog inputs, PWM-capable pins, and the power rails so you can choose the right connection for LEDs, sensors, and small modules. We'll also highlight important safety rules: the board operates at five volts, pins have safe current limits, and certain pins are shared with serial communication. As you learn each part, you'll practice labeling a pinout diagram and answering quick checks that confirm you know which pins to use for which tasks. By the end of this chapter you will be able to read a pinout, identify PWM and analog pins, and explain why mixing three-volt and five-volt connections or overloading a pin can harm the board. Think about a small LED blink project you might build — understanding the pinout makes that first wiring step reliable and repeatable.

These objectives guide what you'll be able to do after this chapter. First, you'll identify the main components on the Uno so you can point to the microcontroller, USB connector, power jack, and common headers. That skill matters because recognizing parts prevents miswiring. Second, you'll distinguish pin types: digital, analog inputs, power rails, and ground. Practically, this prevents connecting a sensor to the wrong pin and saves time troubleshooting. Third, you'll understand pin capabilities such as PWM for variable outputs, serial communication that shares pins zero and one, and the idea of interrupts so you can choose pins suitable for responsive events. Lastly, you'll be able to read a simple pinout diagram and label PWM pins, analog pins, the five-volt rail, and ground. Each objective includes a short verification milestone so you know when you're ready to move on. A common misconception is thinking all pins are identical; in reality, pins have different electrical roles. Keep that in mind as you practice labeling and wiring a basic LED circuit during the hands-on activity.

This second objectives slide shows how you'll practice and verify the skills. You'll print or open an Uno pinout diagram, then label PWM pins, analog inputs, the five-volt rail, and at least two ground pins as a hands-on activity. That practice converts recognition into habit so wiring becomes quicker and safer. You'll also run a simple LED blink test on pin thirteen because the onboard LED provides an immediate confirmation the board and code are working. For PWM practice you'll dim an LED on a PWM-supported pin and observe the analog-like brightness change; this demonstrates how PWM produces a variable output from a digital pin. Finally, you'll answer short assessment questions: which pins support PWM, what's the maximum safe current per pin, and what voltage a HIGH signal represents on an Uno. Checking these answers protects your board and reinforces correct wiring choices. A common misconception is assuming the five-volt pin can safely power motors; in practice you should avoid using the board's five-volt rail for high-current devices.

The ATmega328P is the central microcontroller on the Uno that executes your programs and controls pins. Conceptually, it contains program memory where your sketch is stored, working memory used for variables when the program runs, and a small persistent storage area for values that must survive power cycles. The chapter lists the memory layout: thirty-two kilobytes of flash for program storage, two kilobytes of SRAM for runtime variables, and one kilobyte of EEPROM for persistent data. The chip runs at sixteen megahertz and operates at five volts, meaning its digital HIGH is five volts and LOW is zero volts. A concrete example: when you upload an LED blink sketch, the compiled program lives in flash. As the program runs, counters and state variables live in SRAM. If you want to save a configuration value that remains after a restart, you write it into EEPROM. A common beginner misconception is assuming the microcontroller can safely source large currents for motors or other actuators; the chip's input and output pins are limited in current and must be respected to avoid permanent damage. Takeaway: the ATmega328P is the board's decision maker and its memory and voltage domain shape both how you write programs and how you wire hardware.

The Uno exposes fourteen digital input/output pins numbered zero through thirteen. These pins can be used to read switches, drive LEDs, or control modules by setting them HIGH or LOW. A crucial detail: pins zero and one are also connected to the board's serial communication with the computer. That means when you use the serial port for debugging or upload sketches, those pins may be busy; beginners should avoid using them for other tasks when possible to prevent conflicts. Some pins offer additional capabilities — for example, a subset supports Pulse Width Modulation which we'll cover separately — but the base ability of digital pins is to act as a binary input or output at five volts. A concrete example: to turn an LED on you set its pin HIGH and provide a resistor to limit current; to read a pushbutton you configure a pin as input and check whether it reads HIGH when pressed. A common mistake is assuming any digital pin is suitable for serial communication; only pins zero and one are linked to the onboard serial lines. Closing question: which pins would you avoid using if you plan to use serial debugging during development?

Pulse Width Modulation, or PWM, lets a digital pin mimic analog voltage by switching rapidly between HIGH and LOW. On the Uno, pins three, five, six, nine, ten, and eleven are PWM-capable, typically marked with a tilde. The microcontroller alternates the pin between five volts and zero volts at a fixed frequency, but varies the proportion of time the signal is HIGH versus LOW — that proportion is called duty cycle. When an LED is driven by a PWM pin, a higher duty cycle produces a brighter apparent output because the LED is on for a larger fraction of each cycle. A concrete example: to dim an LED smoothly, you write different duty cycles to a PWM pin and observe brightness change, which looks like analog variation though the pin is digital. A common misconception is that PWM outputs are true analog voltages; in fact they are digital pulses averaged by the LED or a filter to appear analog. A safety note: the pin still obeys current limits, so use an appropriate resistor and avoid drawing excessive current. Takeaway: PWM expands what digital pins can do, letting you control LED brightness or motor speed with careful duty-cycle changes.

The Uno provides six analog input pins labeled A0 through A5. These pins measure a voltage between zero and five volts and convert that voltage into a numeric value using a ten-bit Analog-to-Digital Converter. The conversion maps the measured voltage to a number between zero and one thousand twenty-three. For example, a sensor that outputs two and a half volts would read around halfway through the scale, producing a value close to five hundred. While called analog inputs, these pins can also be used as general-purpose digital pins if you need extra digital input and output. A practical use case is reading a variable resistor or a light sensor to produce values you can use in code to make decisions. A misconception is assuming analog inputs provide infinite precision; because the ADC is ten-bit, it provides discrete steps and not a perfectly smooth voltage reading. Key practice: always ensure the sensor voltage stays in the zero-to-five-volt range; exceeding that range risks damaging the microcontroller. Closing question: how would you convert the ADC reading back into a voltage in your application?

The Uno's power section supplies the voltages your components need and offers multiple connectors. There are 5-volt and 3.3-volt pins used to power small sensors and modules, and several ground pins to complete circuits. The board can be powered over the USB-B connector or an external barrel jack. The USB connector is convenient for programming and low-current power, while the barrel jack supports higher external voltages via the board's regulator.
